Both solutions reach the same answer, p^n + p − 1, and both arithmetic chains are correct:

- Solution A: (p−1) + p^{n−1} + p^{n−1}(p−1) = (p−1) + p^{n−1}·p = p^n + p − 1.
- Solution B: p^{n−1} + (p−1) + p^{n−1}(p−1) = p^{n−1}·p + (p−1) = p^n + p − 1.

The real question is whether the three subgroups are correct, and neither solution justifies that step. Aut(G) is cyclic of order p^{n−1}(p−1), so each divisor corresponds to exactly one subgroup, which makes the orders p−1, p^{n−1}, and p^{n−1}(p−1) plausible candidates. I can't verify from memory which three subgroups the classification theorem actually gives, so the correctness of the shared answer is unconfirmed.

Solution B is somewhat better in presentation. It identifies the subgroups concretely (the p-part, the p′-part, and the full group), which matches the structure of the cyclic group Aut(G). Solution A only lists orders. Neither is more likely correct on the mathematics, since they share the same unverified classification.

WINNER: B
